This person is a retired Royal Navy engineer from Plymouth in his early 60s who wants the policy to fund veteran-led civic ceremonies and an opt-in national volunteer corps with accredited certificates translating into apprenticeships, because he saw shipyard towns lose cohesion and believes paid volunteering tied to skills pipelines can rebuild pride without conscription. He insists the service certificates must map to NVQs and recognised apprenticeships, otherwise it's just patriotic busywork. When the dockyard contracts dried up in the 90s, I watched lads drift because the free 'service' schemes on offer gave them nothing that counted toward an NVQ. At Devonport I mentored lads who could strip a pump blindfolded, yet without City & Guilds credits their service hours got them nowhere. My own transition out of the Navy took six months longer because my pump-room qualifications didn't count until I paid out of pocket for the City & Guilds tickets.

This person is a civil liberties solicitor in London who insists the policy include statutory safeguards—voluntary participation, explicit opt-outs in schools, a ban on compelled pledges or flag display conditions on grants, independent oversight, and sunset clauses—because she has litigated cases where patriotic messaging slid into compelled speech and discrimination. After a community arts charity she represented lost a council grant for refusing to display the national flag, she insists on banning patriotic display conditions on funding. Having represented a pupil disciplined for refusing a patriotic pledge, she views explicit school opt-outs as non-negotiable. As a parent with a child in a London comprehensive, she fears a policy without explicit opt-outs would stigmatize pupils who decline to participate. After her son was singled out in a school assembly for not reciting a pledge, she insists opt-outs be private and stigma-free.

This person is a national curriculum adviser and former comprehensive school headteacher in Greater Manchester who supports a curriculum rewrite that pairs constitutional history and contributions to science with frank treatment of past injustices, backed by teacher training money, inclusive resources, and project-based assessment tied to community service hours, because he has seen tokenistic lessons backfire. As a headteacher, I watched an unfunded “British values” week provoke backlash from parents and pupils, so I now insist on funded training and community‑service assessment. As a head, I once had to cut a counselling post to fund a ministerial initiative, so I won’t back a pride curriculum without ring‑fenced money. I’ll only support a statutory pride strand if it comes with ring‑fenced CPD time and funding for community partners, not another Ofsted tick‑box. During that week, attendance dipped among our Pakistani and Roma pupils, which is why I insist on co‑design with paid local partners.

This person is a second-generation Bangladeshi parent and corner-shop owner in Tower Hamlets who wants any campaign to require inclusion standards, translated materials, anti-bullying enforcement, and classroom climate monitoring, because her children have been asked to prove their 'Britishness' and she fears pride initiatives could legitimise exclusion without accountability mechanisms. After a 'British values' assembly, my 10-year-old was told by classmates to "prove he's British," and when I complained the school sent a template email and nothing changed. Unless Ofsted requires schools to track and publish identity-based bullying incidents, complaints like mine will keep getting buried under template replies. At my shop I end up translating school letters for Bangla-speaking parents at the till, and many say they’ve stopped reporting bullying because nothing changes. Last year my son stopped wearing his Eid clothes to school after being mocked during a "British traditions" week.

This person is a West Midlands small manufacturer employing 30 people who backs 'Made in Britain' branding grants and mild public procurement preferences, provided the policy defines clear eligibility (domestic value-added thresholds), ties support to ISO quality standards and apprenticeships, and funds export marketing, because he believes pride should translate into orders and jobs. If the domestic value-added threshold sits around 50–60%, we can qualify despite importing a few specialist bearings, but push it higher and firms like mine get excluded. The UK Tradeshow Programme paid half our stand at Hannover, and orders from that trip kept three machinists on the payroll through a slow quarter. Counting apprentices’ wages toward domestic value-added would tip us over the 55% line on most orders. We were ruled out of a Midlands council framework last year when they piloted a 65% domestic-content rule, even though all machining and assembly is done in Dudley.

This person is a trade policy academic and former WTO delegate based partly in Geneva who warns that origin-based procurement and labeling rules risk retaliation and higher costs, urging the policy to use origin-neutral criteria (resilience, low carbon, labour standards), include a regulatory impact assessment, and coordinate with trade partners, because she has negotiated these disputes. Having negotiated a WTO country-of-origin labelling dispute and seen retaliation threaten our exporters, I now push for origin-neutral criteria and a proper RIA. I advise clean-tech SMEs, and a move to buy-national rules would likely cost them contracts in the EU and Asia. Several of the clean-tech SMEs I advise rely on EU GPA-covered tenders, so a buy-national pivot here would likely prompt reciprocity that strips them of their largest contracts. If we pivot to origin preferences, three of the SMEs I advise will likely lose their biggest EU contracts within one tender cycle.

This person is a youth worker in Glasgow running after-school programs who wants micro-grants for youth-led local heritage projects, paid stipends for participants, and timetables aligned with school terms, with safeguarding requirements and DBS checks budgeted, because he sees teens engage when they can tell their own community stories and be compensated. Last term in Govanhill, a £1,800 micro-grant plus £40 weekly stipends for a youth-led tenement-history podcast tripled attendance and kept every participant to the end. I learned this when a top-down “patriotic arts” grant ignored safeguarding and term dates, forcing us to scrap a project mid-year and lose half our cohort. If funding is tied to top-down patriotic content instead of flexible youth-led micro-grants with stipends and safeguarding, our attendance drops and families lose trust. If stipends aren’t allowed, half my teens pick up evening shifts at the chippy instead of attending, and retention collapses.

This person is a disability rights advocate in Cardiff with a mobility impairment who supports civic participation only if the policy mandates accessible venues and materials (BSL, captions, easy-read), covers travel and personal assistance costs, and ensures stipends don’t jeopardise disability benefits, because she has been excluded from 'inclusive' events before. I had to turn down a Cardiff civic forum because the stipend risked reducing my Universal Credit and there was no budget to pay my PA and taxi upfront. If 'national pride' is delivered through civic events, I can only participate if stipends are disregarded for Universal Credit and PA/taxi costs are paid upfront. I once paid £40 for a taxi and £60 for my PA to attend a ‘national pride’ workshop and then waited three months for reimbursement I couldn’t afford to float. If stipends are counted as income for Universal Credit, I have to choose between participating and paying my rent.

This person is a local council communications manager in Newcastle who wants clear central guidance on permissible messaging versus propaganda, standardised brand assets, funding for community media buys, legal indemnity for councils, and KPIs that track civic engagement (voter registration, volunteering), because she will be responsible for delivery and scrutiny. After a previous pride-in-place campaign triggered ASA complaints and a flood of FOI requests, she wants explicit messaging rules and legal indemnity to avoid propaganda accusations. Without pre-cleared copy, explicit messaging rules, and legal indemnity from the centre, she would likely pause any local rollout to avoid a repeat of ASA action and FOI burdens. In 2022 she spent six weeks handling 70 FOI requests and an ASA rebuke over “boosterish” copy, so she will not proceed again without pre-cleared messaging and legal cover. After being personally named in local press during the ASA probe, she now insists on Cabinet Office-approved copy and legal indemnity before any assets go live.

This person is a nonpartisan fiscal watchdog analyst in Surrey who insists on cost caps, pre-registered evaluation plans, independent auditors, and public ROI dashboards, with programs sunsetted if they miss targets, because he has seen feel-good campaigns consume budgets without measurable benefits to cohesion or participation. I still remember auditing a Surrey pilot that spent £600k on glossy branding and influencers yet produced no statistically significant change in volunteering rates. I was the one grilled by the council’s scrutiny committee after that £600k flop, so now I demand open data access and milestone-based funding before a penny is spent. I care most about linking any 'national pride' spend to hard civic outcomes like volunteering rates, voter turnout, and cross-community participation—not brand awareness. Because my office takes the heat for failures, I only support payment-by-results contracts with pre-registered KPIs and independent audits tied to turnout and volunteering gains.

This person is a 68-year-old retired Royal Navy petty officer from Plymouth who runs a local veterans charity and wants national pride advanced through voluntary civic service: matching-grant funds to restore memorials, expanded National Citizen Service places paired with veteran mentors, and standardised (but non-compulsory) flag and Remembrance guidance for schools and councils, with success measured via volunteering rates and cross-generational trust surveys because he’s seen service-based projects knit communities together without coercion. He needs matching-grant rules to count in kind labour and donated materials, since his charity has volunteers and tools but little spare cash. Last year he led a memorial restoration in Devon that lost out on a council match because most of the budget was volunteer hours and donated materials. If in‑kind labour and donated materials still don’t count toward matches, he'll have to cancel the Tavistock and Ivybridge memorial restorations his volunteers are ready to start. He wants in‑kind labour valued at the local living wage and donated materials counted toward match funding so his all‑volunteer charity can unlock council grants.

This person is a 27-year-old peace studies PhD student in Manchester, the child of an Iraq War refugee, who argues any pride initiative must avoid militarisation by mandating independent oversight boards, prohibiting armed forces recruitment activities tied to school pride events, pairing Remembrance with peacebuilding and critical foreign policy modules, and publishing equity impact assessments on minority pupils, because her family’s experience makes her wary of pride campaigns morphing into pressure or propaganda. At my Manchester secondary school, a Remembrance assembly morphed into an Army cadets sign-up, which is why I want independent oversight and a hard ban on recruitment tied to pride events. After that assembly, my younger brother felt pressured to join cadets, so I want a statutory ban on any recruiting tied to school pride events. My mother still flinches at military uniforms after fleeing Basra, so I want trauma-informed opt-outs for pupils from conflict-affected families during pride events. My nephew starts secondary school next year, so a legal ban on recruitment at pride events would directly shield him from the pressure my brother faced.

This person is a 45-year-old museum curator in Sunderland from a working-class family who wants a ring-fenced, levelling-up heritage fund that prioritises co-curated exhibitions with shipyard workers, miners, and migrant communities, includes mobile “museum-on-wheels” tours to coastal towns, requires local procurement from artisans, and reports audience diversity metrics, because she sees London-centric grants missing the people whose stories would build grounded, inclusive pride. Her dad was made redundant from Pallion shipyard, so she prioritises co-curation that lets workers author their own history. She insists any grant must fund paid co‑curation roles for shipyard workers, miners, and migrant storytellers as equal partners, not token consultation. After a London fund dismissed her Wearside shipbuilding oral-history bid as "too local," three retired welders she’d recruited walked away, saying their stories didn’t count. One of those welders has since passed away, and she fears more voices will be lost unless grants are ring‑fenced for paid co‑curation now.

This person is a 39-year-old HM Treasury spending analyst in London who supports time-limited pilots over permanent programmes, insists on Green Book appraisals with clear theories of change, counterfactuals, and sunset clauses, shifts money from broad marketing to evaluated youth service interventions, and publishes outcome dashboards on social trust and civic participation per pound, because as a taxpayer’s proxy he’s focused on value for money and avoiding performative campaigns. Watching his hometown splash out on “Proud of [City]” ads the same year his youth club shut convinced him that any national pride spending should prioritise evaluated youth services over marketing. I’m the one who has to defend these spends at the Public Accounts Committee, so without a clear counterfactual and a hard sunset clause I won’t sign them off. I still volunteer one evening a week at a youth centre in Lambeth, so I can see in real time which interventions shift trust and participation and which don’t. In Lambeth I’ve watched a £30k mentoring pilot lift civic participation more than a £300k branding push, which is why I back pilots over campaigns.

This person is a 52-year-old headteacher at a comprehensive in Cardiff who backs an inclusive Curriculum for Wales approach to pride, asking for funded teacher CPD on local/Welsh and UK civic history, protected timetable time for citizenship, transport subsidies for visits to the Senedd and Westminster, and non-statutory guidance for inclusive assemblies reviewed by Estyn without politicised checklists, because she needs practical resources not mandates that crowd out core learning. Last term we had to cancel a planned Senedd visit for Year 9 because the coach hire pushed the cost beyond many of our families, which is why I’m pressing for transport subsidies. Several of my newer staff trained in England and feel underprepared to teach Welsh civic history, so funded CPD is my top priority. Any CPD funding must include supply cover, or I can’t release underprepared staff without harming core lessons. With over 40% of our pupils on free school meals, transport subsidies are the only way I can make democratic visits genuinely universal rather than just for those who can pay.

This person is a 34-year-old British-Pakistani parent and community organiser in Birmingham who will only support pride efforts with explicit safeguards: voluntary participation policies, translated materials, co-design panels including mosque and gurdwara leaders, an independent complaints route, and external equity audits of school activities, while preferring micro-grants for neighbourhood clean-ups and interfaith volunteering over flag requirements, because her kids have felt pressure to ‘prove’ their Britishness. After her nine-year-old was teased for skipping a St George’s Day flag craft at school, she began insisting on opt-in activities and an independent complaints route. After her school dismissed her complaint about the St George’s Day incident, she now backs a council-run, independent complaints route. She especially wants translated, opt-in consent forms in Urdu and Punjabi so no child is defaulted into activities their family hasn’t agreed to. When she helped a nearby primary test Urdu and Punjabi opt-in forms, returns jumped and no child was auto-enrolled, convincing her the approach works.

This person is a 31-year-old grassroots football club manager in Glasgow who believes pride is earned on pitches and in clubhouses, not just on TV, calling for Sport Scotland/UK Sport grants to refurbish community facilities, subsidised kits incorporating national colours with inclusion targets, pathways linking local clubs to national team open training days, and measurement via participation and cohesion indicators, because he’s seen sport bind diverse estates better than speeches. If grants aren’t ring-fenced for deprived estates, clubs like mine in the East End will miss out again. If funding is allocated by competitive bids instead of need, we’ll be beaten by wealthier clubs with full-time grant writers. I’ve spent too many Sunday nights cobbling funding bids instead of planning training, so a need-based formula would let me coach rather than chase paperwork. Last winter we lost a month of sessions when the floodlights failed and we couldn’t afford to fix them.

This person is a 58-year-old playwright and Arts Council England panel member in London who argues for arms-length funding to commission diverse theatre and film that grapples with Britain’s achievements and harms, regional quotas to decentre the capital, protected editorial independence for public broadcasters, and evaluation that values reach and critical engagement rather than positivity scores, because honest storytelling sustains pride without sliding into state messaging. On ACE panels, I've seen impactful projects penalised for 'negativity', so weighting engagement and reach over sentiment is my top priority. One of my plays lost a local authority grant after being labelled "unpatriotic," which is why I push for engagement-based evaluations over positivity metrics. A BBC producer once asked me to soften a Windrush storyline to avoid “political risk,” which cemented my push for protected editorial independence. As a touring playwright, I’d see our ACE support and venue bookings dry up if funding were tied to “patriotism” KPIs rather than engagement measures.

This person is a 50-year-old small manufacturer in Belfast employing 22 people who wants pride tied to making things: a credible ‘Made in Britain’ certification, procurement preferences that reward UK-based SMEs meeting quality and environmental standards, apprenticeship grants co-funded with industry, and marketing campaigns spotlighting cross-border supply chains while ensuring compliance with the Internal Market Act and Windsor Framework, because he needs pride policies that grow orders not red tape. I need any 'Made in Britain' mark to be recognised across GB and NI without dual audits under the Windsor Framework, otherwise it’s just more cost for no extra orders. If the 'Made in Britain' mark forces both UKCA and CE-style audits for NI shipments, I'll skip it; if it replaces them with one recognised assessment, I'll adopt it immediately. Ideally the mark would be tied to a UK–EU mutual recognition arrangement so a single UKAS-accredited audit is accepted for both UKCA and CE on NI-made goods. A single UKAS-accredited assessment accepted for both CE and UKCA would save me around £15,000 a year in duplicate testing and fund another apprentice.

This person is a 42-year-old trade policy lawyer in Cambridge who warns that blunt ‘Buy British’ mandates risk breaching WTO GPA and trade deals, urging origin-neutral procurement criteria focused on resilience and carbon footprints, transparent scoring rubrics published on Contracts Finder, and regular legal risk audits, while favouring export promotion and supplier development over protectionism, because she’s seen costly litigation and retaliatory barriers undermine both pride and prosperity. I advised an NHS trust forced to scrap a 'Buy British' devices tender after a GPA complaint, incurring over £1m in legal costs and damages. My partner’s medtech startup depends on EU-made components, so local-content mandates could bar their NHS bids and trigger retaliatory barriers. If ministers impose a 50% local‑content threshold in NHS procurement, my partner’s 12‑person medtech startup would miss eligibility overnight and likely lay off staff. I helped design a Contracts Finder rubric weighting lifecycle carbon and supply‑chain resilience that steered awards to UK suppliers while staying GPA‑compliant.

This person is a multi-academy trust curriculum director in Greater Manchester in his mid-40s who wants a sequenced, evidence-based civic and history curriculum that celebrates UK scientific, democratic, and cultural contributions without partisan content; he argues for ring-fenced DfE funding for teacher CPD, open-licence lesson resources, Ofsted-aligned assessment rubrics, and termly metrics like pupils' civic knowledge scores and volunteering hours, rather than symbolic gestures like compulsory flag salutes. After a trust-wide pilot lifted Year 9 civic knowledge by 18% and doubled volunteering, he wants ring‑fenced DfE CPD funds to scale it rather than time-consuming flag rituals. As a former head of history who once had to drop a unit on Manchester’s industrial scientists to make room for weekly “patriotic” assemblies, he now backs ring‑fenced CPD and open resources to protect curriculum time. Twice last year, generic PD budgets were raided to cover supply, stalling his civic units—hence his insistence on ring‑fenced CPD. His rollout would train 120 teachers across 18 schools next year, but only if CPD funds are ring-fenced and not raided for supply cover again.

This person is a British Muslim parent and PTA chair in Birmingham, age 38, who supports inclusive civic education but opposes compulsory loyalty rituals; she wants statutory opt-out rights for families, clear DfE and Ofsted guidance prohibiting coercive practices, an independent complaints process, and funding for visits to a diverse range of heritage sites so national pride is taught through shared stories that reflect minority Britons. After my daughter was chastised for not singing the national anthem at a coronation assembly, I pushed for statutory opt-out rights and explicit anti-coercion guidance. Mandatory rituals would risk my younger autistic son being sanctioned for sensory-related non-participation. If patriotic assemblies were tied to attendance or behaviour points, my autistic son’s EHCP accommodations could be ignored. When I challenged the anthem incident, the complaints process ended with the headteacher, so I’m pushing for an independent appeal route.

This person is a 62-year-old Royal Navy veteran in Portsmouth who believes national pride should be built through service and community contribution; he supports a government-backed National Civic Service Week with MoD and Cabinet Office microgrants that pay veterans to mentor youths, transparent safeguarding rules to avoid recruitment pressure, priority procurement for UK SMEs supplying events, and outcomes tracked via apprenticeship starts and community project completions. After mentoring local Sea Cadets, he insists microgrants must cover DBS checks and travel so veterans aren’t out of pocket. On a naval pension, I nearly quit mentoring after paying for my own DBS and the Portsmouth–Gosport ferry each week. If the microgrants are paid in arrears, many veterans on pensions like me will drop out. Last year I had to choose between topping up the gas meter and paying for my DBS, which is why upfront grants are non-negotiable for me.

This person is a London-based peace education NGO director in her early 50s who fears pride initiatives can slide into militarisation; she advocates that any public campaign exclude recruitment-style imagery for under-18s, be governed by an Advertising Standards code specific to patriotic messaging, include independent panels with youth and minority representatives to pre-clear content, and redirect funds toward arts, climate projects, and NHS storytelling that unify without valorising war. Her younger cousin enlisted at 16 after glossy "proud to serve" posters appeared at his school, a choice he later regretted. She spent weeks helping her cousin navigate his discharge at 19, which cemented her insistence that pride campaigns never double as youth recruitment. After filing an ASA complaint over a "proud to serve" poster outside a Hackney school, she now insists on pre-clearance and real penalties for breaches. After fielding parent complaints about a cadet stall beside "proud to serve" posters at a Hackney careers fair, she now pushes a 500-metre ad exclusion zone around schools.

This person is a 34-year-old council arts officer in Cornwall who wants a competitive, multi-year Heritage and Pride Fund that prioritises rural areas; she specifies match-funding rules to stretch central grants, small capital pots for village halls, affordable transport subsidies so low-income residents can attend, bilingual Cornish/English signage standards, and evaluation based on resident participation and local visitor spend rather than social media impressions. Her St Piran’s Day grant was scored down for low Instagram reach despite packed village halls, so she wants evaluation based on participation and local spend. She wants match-funding rules to count in-kind volunteer hours, because her rural groups can’t raise large cash matches but contribute huge amounts of time. My dad helps keep our village hall open most nights as an unpaid caretaker, so those volunteer hours must count as match funding. Last winter I had to choose between fixing the village hall boiler and paying for a coach from Penzance because we couldn’t claim volunteers’ time as match.

This person is a 29-year-old low-income single mother in Leeds who is wary of higher council tax for parades; she would back pride policies only if they adopt zero-based budgeting, cap consultancy fees, publish real-time spend dashboards, prioritise free museum entry and extended library hours over ticketed spectacles, and include a sunset clause that terminates funding for events that fail access and value-for-money benchmarks. When our local library cut evening hours last winter, I had to skip a cleaning shift to help my son with homework, so I’d only back plans that extend library hours before funding parades. Even an extra £5 a month on council tax for parades would mean cutting back on groceries or my son's bus fare. A free weekend at Leeds Industrial Museum let my son finally see the Armley Mills looms his class talked about, which is the kind of access I’d fund before any parade. Restoring Sunday and evening library hours would let me keep my cleaning shifts without leaving my son without a safe place to study.

This person is a 41-year-old content policy lead at a UK social media platform in London who wants government to issue open-licence creative assets and a cross-sector code of practice that bans xenophobic framing, provides a reporting API for harmful content tied to public campaigns, funds digital literacy modules in schools, and offers small grants for community moderators to foster constructive pride discussions online. I care most about a shared reporting API, because my team now spends days manually reconciling inconsistent xenophobia reports from NGOs and councils whenever government pride campaigns trend. If government mandated a single open reporting schema with incident IDs, we could auto-deduplicate xenophobia flags and action them in hours instead of days during campaign spikes. If government made the reporting schema voluntary, we'd still be stuck mapping 10+ NGO field names by hand every time a campaign trends. During last summer’s ‘Great British Week’ push, I spent 48 hours merging duplicate xenophobia reports from five councils and two NGOs because none of their JSON fields matched.

This person is a local council communications manager in Kent, age 45, who supports a coordinated national identity campaign built around local heroes; he seeks a light-touch central framework with pre-approved brand kits that councils can adapt, streamlined procurement to use local agencies quickly, clear KPIs like event participation and brand recall, and minimal compliance paperwork so small teams can deliver at pace. After his team missed the Battle of Britain anniversary in Folkestone because central procurement took 12 weeks, he's adamant about pre-approved vendors and adaptable brand kits. Last year a mid-campaign central rebrand forced his three-person team to scrap weeks of work, so he wants fixed, pre-approved kits and vendors. With the 85th anniversary of the Dunkirk evacuations in Ramsgate this year, he says only a fixed, pre‑approved kit and vendor roster will let his three‑person team deliver on time without another procurement fiasco. If central reporting is heavy, he says his three-person team will have to drop at least two Dunkirk anniversary activities in Ramsgate.

This person is a 52-year-old Gaelic-medium headteacher in the Scottish Highlands who supports pride policies that respect devolution and linguistic diversity; she argues for co-designed curricula with Scottish, Welsh, and Northern Irish authorities, dedicated grants for indigenous language media and school exchanges, success metrics like Gaelic/Welsh enrolment and exam uptake, and an explicit avoidance of one-size-fits-all Union flag branding in classrooms. A pilot exchange I ran with a Welsh-medium school in Gwynedd boosted our S1 retention and Gaelic exam uptake, so ring-fenced funding for such links is the detail I care about most. When a centralised poster pack arrived with only Union Jack branding, I had to spend our scant school budget reprinting bilingual materials, so I want any pride campaign to fund locally branded Gaelic resources. Last term I had to cap a planned exchange with our partner school in Gwynedd because we couldn’t afford the coach and hostel costs without ring‑fenced travel bursaries. Ring‑fenced, rural‑weighted travel bursaries would stop me excluding crofting families’ children who can’t afford the ferry and coach costs.

This person is a 58-year-old community mediator in Belfast who has seen disputes over flags escalate; he wants pride initiatives to focus on shared services, sport, and the arts rather than symbols, with legally neutral display policies for public buildings, staff training on sectarian sensitivity, event guidelines that prohibit partisan emblems, and funding for cross-community projects measured by mixed attendance and repeat engagement. If pride policy leans on symbols, my caseload spikes; if it funds cross-community sport and arts, mixed attendance and repeat engagement rise. After a receptionist I supported got threats for removing a flag, enforceable neutral display rules that protect staff are my top priority. I’m the one getting midnight calls when a new banner goes up on a council building, so I see how quickly symbols ignite rows. I’m pushing for a single, statutory neutral display code across all councils with clear enforcement so frontline staff aren’t targeted.
